name: NestJs
scope: A person with BEGINNER proficiency level in NestJs as a competency should be able to understand what NestJS is, its modular architecture, dependency injection, and how it builds on Node.js/Express, recognize building blocks (modules, controllers, services, providers, pipes, guards, interceptors), and basic request–response lifecycle. They should organize code using the Nest CLI, create and use modules, controllers, and services, define basic routes and handlers with HTTP method decorators, use DTOs for data shape, apply simple validation with class-validator/class-transformer, and handle basic error responses using HttpException and built-in exceptions. They should manage in-memory data in services for CRUD operations, use async/await in controllers/services, and understand the difference between controller and service responsibilities. Awareness of authentication (guards, JWT, Passport), testing (Jest, CLI-generated tests), logging (console, Logger), configuration (environment variables, ConfigModule), and deployment basics (Node.js runtime, process.env) is expected. They should follow best practices for code organization, naming, and separation of concerns, be able to run and test endpoints locally, use basic Git workflows, communicate design choices, and have awareness of documentation tools like Swagger.

{"sections":[{"name":"NestJS Core Fundamentals","scope_included":"- Understand what NestJS is and when to use it (framework for building scalable server-side Node.js applications using TypeScript and OOP/FP/FP patterns)
- Recognize key design philosophies of NestJS: modular architecture, dependency injection, convention over configuration
- Understand how NestJS builds on top of Node.js and Express (or Fastify) without needing deep Express knowledge
- Know the high-level building blocks: modules, controllers, providers/services, pipes, guards, interceptors (at least by name and basic role)
- Understand the basic request–response lifecycle in a NestJS application at a conceptual level
- Be aware that NestJS encourages strongly-typed code using TypeScript and decorators
- Recognize common NestJS use cases: REST APIs/HTTP backends, simple microservices, backend for web/mobile apps
- Understand basic terminology: handler, route, middleware, DTO, provider, dependency injection container","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Application Structure & Modules","scope_included":"- Understand the default project structure generated by Nest CLI (main.ts, app.module.ts, app.controller.ts, app.service.ts, etc.)
- Know what a NestJS module is and why it exists (logical grouping of related components)
- Be able to identify the root module (AppModule) in a basic project
- Understand, at a simple level, the @Module decorator and its main properties: imports, controllers, providers, exports
- Be able to add a simple feature module to an existing project using CLI or manually (e.g., UsersModule)
- Understand that modules help with organization and separation of concerns, even if not yet designing complex module boundaries
- Recognize the difference between feature modules (e.g., UsersModule) and the root module (AppModule)
- Be able to keep a small application organized into at least 1–2 simple modules instead of placing everything in AppModule","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Controllers, Routing & Request Handling","scope_included":"- Understand the purpose of controllers: handling incoming HTTP requests and returning responses
- Know how to define a simple controller class using the @Controller decorator
- Be able to define basic route handlers using @Get, @Post, @Put, @Delete, @Patch decorators
- Understand how route paths work at controller level (e.g., @Controller('users')) and method level (e.g., @Get(':id'))
- Know how to access route parameters via @Param, query parameters via @Query, and request body via @Body
- Be able to return basic JSON objects or primitive types from controller methods
- Understand the difference between HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) in the context of RESTful endpoints
- Be aware of how NestJS maps controller return values to HTTP responses (auto-serialization of objects to JSON by default)
- Know that controllers should generally delegate business logic to services rather than implement logic inline (even if still learning to consistently apply it)
- Understand default HTTP status codes used by NestJS (e.g., 200 OK for GET, 201 Created for POST) and how to override them using @HttpCode when needed","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Providers, Services & Basic Dependency Injection","scope_included":"- Understand what a provider is in NestJS and why providers exist (encapsulate reusable logic, injectable into other classes)
- Know how to create a simple service class annotated with @Injectable
- Be able to connect a controller to a service by injecting the service via the constructor
- Understand the basics of dependency injection: NestJS creates and manages instances, rather than using "new" directly
- Recognize that providers must be registered in a module’s providers array to be available for injection
- Be able to implement a simple in-memory data store in a service (e.g., array-based CRUD operations) without persistence
- Understand the difference between controller responsibilities (handling HTTP & mapping requests) and service responsibilities (business logic, data access)
- Be aware that provider scope (singleton vs request-scoped) exists conceptually, even if always using default singleton behavior at this level","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"DTOs, Validation & Basic Data Handling","scope_included":"- Understand the concept of a Data Transfer Object (DTO) for defining the shape of data sent to/returned from APIs
- Be able to create simple DTO classes using TypeScript (interfaces or classes) to describe request payloads
- Have basic awareness of using class-validator and class-transformer with NestJS for validation, even if not mastering complex rules
- Be able to apply @Body() with a DTO type to strongly-type incoming request data in controller methods
- Understand the benefit of DTOs for input validation, maintainability, and clear contracts between client and server
- Recognize that validation pipes can be used to validate incoming data, with awareness of ValidationPipe as a built-in option
- Be able to handle basic scenarios like required vs optional fields at a conceptual level
- Understand basic serialization/JSON structure returned from controllers and how it maps to DTOs or simple objects","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Basic Error Handling & HTTP Responses","scope_included":"- Understand the difference between successful and error HTTP responses at a high level (2xx vs 4xx vs 5xx)
- Be aware of NestJS HttpException class and built-in exceptions like NotFoundException, BadRequestException
- Be able to throw a simple HTTP exception from within a controller or service when a resource is not found or input is invalid
- Understand that unhandled errors typically result in 500 Internal Server Error
- Know that NestJS has a global exception filter mechanism (at awareness level), even if only using the default behavior
- Be able to return basic responses with simple structures: { message: '...', data: ... }
- Understand how NestJS automatically sets HTTP status codes for common scenarios (e.g., POST creating resources) and how exceptions map to specific codes","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Asynchronous Programming & Request Flow Basics in NestJS","scope_included":"- Have basic understanding of async/await in TypeScript/JavaScript and how it is used in NestJS controllers and services
- Be able to write simple async controller methods that await service calls (e.g., database-like operations, even if mocked)
- Understand that NestJS can handle asynchronous operations without blocking the event loop when written correctly
- Know the difference between synchronous return values and Promises at a conceptual level
- Be aware that most real-world service methods in NestJS are async when interacting with I/O (databases, HTTP calls), even if they are currently replaced with stubs or in-memory data at beginner level","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"State Management & Simple Data Access (Non-persistent)","scope_included":"- Be able to manage simple in-memory collections (arrays, maps) inside services to simulate data storage
- Implement basic CRUD-style operations in services (create, read, update, delete) without integrating external databases yet
- Understand that in-memory data is reset when the server restarts and that persistent storage will require databases or external systems (awareness only)
- Know how to structure simple service methods like createUser, findUserById, updateUser, deleteUser in a way that can later be swapped to real persistence
- Be aware that more advanced integrations (ORMs, database connections) exist but are out of scope for a beginner","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Basic NestJS Best Practices (Beginner Level)","scope_included":"- Keep controllers focused on networking concerns (parsing input, returning responses) and avoid heavy business logic in them
- Place reusable logic inside services/providers to encourage separation of concerns
- Organize code into feature modules instead of putting all files into the root module
- Use consistent naming conventions for files and classes (e.g., *.controller.ts, *.service.ts, *.module.ts)
- Avoid using any type unnecessarily; prefer basic TypeScript types (string, number, boolean, interfaces) where possible
- Keep functions and classes small and focused on a single responsibility where feasible
- Understand that hardcoding values is acceptable for learning, but configuration or environment variables will be preferred later
- Begin to write clear, descriptive method and variable names that reflect their purpose
- Avoid over-optimizing; focus on clarity and readability of NestJS code at this stage","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Security & Authentication (Awareness Level)","scope_included":"- Understand that production NestJS applications typically require authentication and authorization, even if not implementing them yet
- Be aware that NestJS uses guards (e.g., AuthGuard) as a key mechanism for protecting routes
- Know that JWT, sessions, or other strategies can be used for authentication in NestJS (awareness only)
- Recognize that handling passwords and sensitive data securely is important and should not be done with plain text storage
- Be aware that NestJS provides integrations and patterns for authentication (e.g., with Passport), to be learned in later proficiency levels","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Testing (Awareness Level)","scope_included":"- Be aware that NestJS supports unit testing and e2e testing out of the box with Jest
- Recognize that the Nest CLI can generate test files alongside controllers and services
- Understand, conceptually, that tests help verify controllers and services behave as expected
- Know that more advanced testing techniques (mocks, dependency injection for tests) will come at later proficiency levels","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Observability & Logging (Beginner Level)","scope_included":"- Understand that logging is important for debugging and monitoring a NestJS application
- Know how to use basic logging features (e.g., console.log) and be aware that NestJS has a built-in Logger class
- Recognize that logs should not expose sensitive data
- Be aware that more advanced monitoring, metrics, and structured logging exist but are for higher proficiency levels","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Tooling, CLI & Project Setup","scope_included":"- Install NestJS CLI globally (e.g., via npm i -g @nestjs/cli) and understand its basic purpose
- Use the Nest CLI to create a new project (nest new project-name) and navigate the generated structure
- Be able to start the development server (npm run start / npm run start:dev) and understand the difference between dev and regular start scripts at a basic level
- Generate basic building blocks using CLI commands: controllers, modules, services (nest generate controller, service, module)
- Understand that the CLI helps enforce conventions and consistent file structure across the project
- Know how to run the application and access exposed HTTP endpoints via a browser or simple API client (e.g., Postman, curl, or similar)
- Have basic familiarity with package.json scripts and dependencies relevant to NestJS
- Be able to install simple additional packages required for beginner-level tasks (e.g., class-validator, class-transformer, if used)
- Understand that TypeScript compilation (via tsc or underlying Nest build steps) turns NestJS code into JavaScript for Node.js execution
- Recognize basic configuration in tsconfig.json at an awareness level (e.g., module, target) without deep customization","is_non_core_section":true},{"name":"Configuration, Environments & Simple Deployment Awareness","scope_included":"- Understand that configuration (e.g., ports, database URLs) should typically be externalized via environment variables in real applications
- Know how to change the listening port or basic settings in main.ts or simple config variables for a beginner app
- Be aware that NestJS has ConfigModule and other configuration helpers, even if not yet using them deeply
- Understand the high-level idea of different environments (development vs production), even if only running locally
- Be aware that deployment involves building the NestJS app and running it on a Node.js runtime (e.g., on a server or cloud platform), at conceptual level only
- Recognize that process.env can be used to access environment variables in Node/Nest
- Understand that additional deployment tools (Docker, CI/CD pipelines, PM2, etc.) exist but are for higher proficiency levels","is_non_core_section":true},{"name":"Collaboration, Documentation & Working in a NestJS Codebase","scope_included":"- Be able to read and understand simple existing NestJS code (controllers, modules, services) written by others
- Follow project conventions for folder structure, naming, and module organization when adding new files
- Write basic inline comments to explain non-obvious logic in controllers and services
- Be aware that API documentation tools such as Swagger (via @nestjs/swagger) exist and are commonly used, even if not yet generating full docs
- Understand how to run and test API endpoints locally to verify changes before sharing code
- Use basic Git workflows to commit changes to NestJS projects with clear, concise commit messages (awareness of version control practices)
- Communicate simple design choices to team members (e.g., why a new controller or service was added) using correct NestJS terminology
- Be open to feedback on code structure (e.g., moving logic from controller to service) and willing to refactor simple parts of the codebase","is_non_core_section":true}]}
